title: Watching a volcano: how scientists read the warning signs
description: Volcanoes rarely erupt without grumbling first. Long before any lava appears, the mountain swells, shivers and breathes out different gases — and teams of scientists are listening for exactly those whispers.

body.heading: The mountain swells and shivers
paragraphs: As magma pushes up inside a volcano, the ground above it can bulge — sometimes by centimetres, sometimes by a metre or more. Scientists track that swelling with satellite measurements and tiltmeters on the slopes, the way you might watch a balloon slowly inflating and know it cannot inflate forever.

At the same time, small earthquakes multiply under the mountain as rock cracks to let the magma through. A seismometer network hears every shiver, and a quiet volcano that suddenly records hundreds of small quakes a day is a volcano clearing its throat.

body.heading: Breathing out clues
paragraphs: A volcano's gases change as magma rises. Instruments — some flown through the plume, some sniffing from the ground — measure gases such as sulphur dioxide; a sharp rise can mean fresh magma is nearing the surface and releasing its fizz, like a shaken bottle about to be opened.

None of these signs alone proves an eruption is coming, and volcanoes sometimes grumble and go back to sleep. So observatories weigh them together — swelling plus quakes plus gas plus heat — before warning the people who live in the mountain's shadow.

body.heading: Why the watching matters
paragraphs: Those warnings save lives: towns can be evacuated days before an eruption when the signs are read in time, and the famous forecasts of the late twentieth century showed that a watched volcano is far less deadly than an unwatched one.

There are roughly a thousand-plus volcanoes on land considered potentially active, and not all can be watched closely. That is why satellites now keep a tireless eye on the remote ones — so no mountain has to grumble unheard.

takeaway: Scientists forecast eruptions by combining four clues — ground swelling, multiplying small earthquakes, changing gases and heat — because a volcano usually whispers before it shouts.
